obic glycolysis. In this text the metabolism of glucose to pyruvate with further oxidation will be referred to simply as glycolysis.
Many cell types will convert glucose to lactate regardless of oxygen availability and this will be referred to as aerobic glycolysis.
The classic example of such a cell is the mammalian red blood cell which, lacking mitochondria, is unable to carry out oxidative
metabolism. A number of other tissues such as some muscles, the renal cortex, and a number of other cell types, including tumors,
also exhibit high rates of aerobic glycolysis, widely known as the Warburg effect.
